title: Tikam Singh vs . on 14 September, 2009
full_text: Tikam Singh vs . on 14 September, 2009 1 IN THE COURT OF SH. VIVEK KUMAR GULIA METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE - 1 [East] KARKARDOOMA COURTS, DELHI In the matter of: Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh C.C. No. 3923/07 PS: Bhajanpura JUDGMENT 1. The serial number of the case : 81/2005 2. The date of complaint : 29.04.2005 3. Name of the complainant : Tikam Singh S/o. Sh. Budh Prakash, R/o. Mohalla Ratan Nagar, (Near Romesh Cinema) Baghpat Road, Meerut, UP. 4. The name, parentage Birbal Singh, and residence of accused : S/o. Sh. Bhola Shanker, R/o. H. No. C-265/B, Gali No. 10, Bhajanpura, Delhi. 5. Offence complained of : U/s. 138 N. I. Act . 6. Plea of the accused : Pleaded not guilty. 7. Final Order : Convicted. 8. Case reserved for order : 24.08.2009. 9. Date of such order : 14.09.2009. Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 2 REASONS FOR THE DECISION: 1. The accused was put to the trial as a result present complaint filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (in short 'the Act'). The facts of the case, in nutshell, are these. It is the complaint case that Rs. One Lac was advanced to accused on his request by complainant on 31.01.2005 and in discharge of his legal liability, accused handed over a cheque bearing No. 734226 dt. 31.01.2005 for Rs. 1,00,000/-, drawn on Punjab National Bank, Yamuna Vihar, Delhi, but on presentation, the same was returned back with the remarks 'insufficient funds'. Thereafter, legal notice dated 12.03.2005 was issued to accused who refused to accept it. Therefore, the accused, as he failed to make the payment within stipulated period, has committed an offence punishable under section 138 of the Act and u/s. 420 IPC. With aforesaid facts, complainant prayed for prosecution and punishment of accused in accordance with law. 2. Substance of accusation in the form of written notice u/s 251 Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 ( Cr.P.C .) was read over and explained to accused on 18.07.2006, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 3. In post summoning evidence, complainant stepped into Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 3 witness box as CW1 and reiterated the facts mentioned in the complaint by way of his affidavit and proved the documents, i.e., cheque in question Ex.CW1/A, memo regarding presentation of the cheque for encashment Ex.CW1/B, cheque returning memo EX.CW1/C, legal notice dt. 12.03.2005 EX.CW1/D, Regd. Post receipt dt. 15.03.05 EX.CW1/D1, UPC receipt dt. 16.03.05 EX.CW1/D2, envelop (returned back) EX.CW1/D3, AD card EX.CW1/D4 and other documents of complainant's bank Ex.CW1/D5 & Ex.CW1/D6. CW2, Rajender Singh, Manager, PNB, Bhajanpura, proved the relevant entries of cheque returning register as Ex.CW2/1 and cheque returning memo EX.CW1/C. CW3, Baldev Singh, Clerk, Syndicate Bank, Baghpat Road, Meerut, proved the relevant entry in collection register as Ex.CW3/1. 4. Accused was questioned generally about the case put forward by the complainant against him and his statement was recorded U/s. 313 Cr. P. C., wherein it is stated that cheque in question was not issued by him in discharge of any legal liability. It is explained that cheque book containing the cheque in question was lost and complainant misused the same. Further, it is mentioned that all the entries in the cheque in question except the signature have not filled up by him. 5. Accused showed his willingness to lead defence evidence Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 4 but failed to adduce evidence in any form and ultimately defence evidence was ordered to be closed on 18.03.2009. 6. I have heard the Bar and perused the record. 7. The most emphasized defensive plea of accused is that cheque in question was not issued in favour of the complainant. It is alleged that the signed cheque was misplaced and same has been misused by the complainant. It is also argued that accused has no direct relation with the complainant and cheque being without any consideration, complaint case be dismissed. However, it can be seen that except the word of the mouth of accused, there is not an iota of evidence on record to suggest that cheque was not issued by accused in favour of complainant to discharge of his liability. There is no explanation as to from where the cheque was misplaced and how it came into the hands of complainant. Further, why any report to police authorities or bank was not given is not made clear. In brief, no ocular or documentary evidence has been produced to substantiate the plea taken by accused. During cross-examination of complainant (CW1), it came on record that both the parties used to visit the house of one Gajender Singh Sangwan at Meerut and since accused was in need of money for making a bid in tender for scraps, cheque amount was given to him on interest @ 2% p.m. It is mentioned that cheque was handed over on 31.01.2005 and no Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 5 loan agreement was executed between the parties. Further, complainant denied the suggestion of accused that cheque book signed by accused was misplaced and blank cheque in question was misused. Thus, it appears that complainant has withstood the test of cross-examination and accused failed to bring anything on record to demolish the case of complainant. 8. Another issue raised by defence side is pertaining to service of legal notice. It is contended that the statutory legal notice was not served on accused, therefore, complaint is liable to dismissed. It is argued that postal endorsement "unclaimed/suchna de di gai hai" dt. 16.03.2005 cannot be considered to be deemed service on accused in absence of report as to where and to whom the intimation was given by the postman. In my view, this plea of accused is without any substance. When his address has not been disputed by accused, there can not be any doubt that intimation about the regd. post envelop was given to addressee or his family member at the address mentioned thereon. Further, on this issue, it has been categorically held by Supreme Court in the case of K. Bhaskaran Vs. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan cited as (1999) 7 SCC 510 that : "...Thus, when a notice is returned by the sendee as unclaimed such date would be the commencing date in reckoning the period of 15 days contemplated in Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 6 clause (c) to the proviso of section 138 of the Act. Of course, such reckoning would be without prejudice to the right of the drawer of the cheque to show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address. In the present case the accused did not even attempt to discharge the burden to rebut the aforesaid presumption". Further, it has been laid down in re: Bhaskaran Vs. Betan (1999) 3 Ker LT 440; Joseph Jose Vs. J Baby 2002 Cr.LJ 4392 (Ker) that : "The endorsement 'unclaimed' can be taken as refusal. Sending of notice to the correct address of the accused and return of the same with endorsement 'unclaimed' are sufficient for the purpose of due compliance of sec. 138 (b) . Burden to prove non-tender of the article is on the accused." In view of these case-laws, there remains no doubt that accused was required to discharge the burden to rebut the legal presumption of deemed service of legal notice on him, but no effort was made by him in this regard. 9. Another point raised from defence side is relating to privity of contract between the parties. It is contended that the complainant failed to prove his relationship with accused and therefore, no question arises as to borrowing money from him. In this regard, it can be observed that complainant has named one Gajender Singh, at whose house parties used to meet, in his Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 7 cross-examination. Accused has not denied this fact by way of any suggestion. Moreover, the burden was on accused to rebut the fact that the complainant had acquaintance with him and same has not been discharged. Thus, this ground of argument also fails. 10. Further, it is argued that complainant failed to prove the fact that cheque was dishonoured by banker of accused on account of insufficient funds since photocopy of collection register has been produced by CW3. This plea deserves rejection outrightly considering that the photocopy of the relevant page of cheque collection register was exhibited (Ex.CW3/1) and accused was required to raise the objection about the admissibility of this document at the time when it was marked as Exhibit. Otherwise also, no suggestion was put to complainant doubting the fact of presenting and dishonouring of cheque in question. 11. The complainant case was also challenged on the ground that since the entries on the cheque in question except the signature are not in the handwriting of accused, it gives strength to the defence plea that the complainant has misused the cheque. After carefully examining the cheque in question, it appears to me that all the entries except the name of payee have been filled up by the same person. Since the signature on the cheque in question has not been disputed by accused, it can be Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 8 concluded that the amount and date columns have also been completed by him only. As far as the name of payee is concerned, there is no legal requirement that same should be in the handwriting of drawer of the cheque. Moreover, no effort has been made by the accused to prove that the entries of the cheque in question are not in his handwriting. Thus, this objection also deserves dismissal. 12. Lastly, it is vehemently argued that complaint has not been filed within limitation period. To decide this aspect of the matter, the relevant events upto the filing of the complaint are summarized as under: Cheque presented for encashment - 03.02.2005. Cheque returned unpaid by banker of accused (PNB) - 12.02.05. Information sent to manager of accused's bank at Baghpat qua unpaid cheque - 16.02.05. Legal notice dt. 12.03.05 dispatched - 15.03.05 Endorsement of "unclaimed/information given" made - 16.03.05. Complaint filed on 29.04.2005. 13. As per section 138 of the Act, the payee is required to make a demand for the payment of cheque amount by giving a Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 9 notice in writing to the drawer of cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of cheque as unpaid and thereafter if drawer of the cheque fails to make payment within 15 days after receiving the said notice, offence under section 138 of the Act is deemed to have been committed. Further section 142 of the Act speaks that after non-payment, complaint is required to be made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arose under clause (c) of the Proviso to sec. 138 of the Act. If we give conjoint reading to both the above mentioned provisions of the Act, then it can be concluded that the complaint has to be filed within one month after expiry of 15 days of the receipt of the notice by the drawer. 14. The period of limitation has to be reckoned from the date of accrual of the cause of action. No doubt true it is, that a cause of action will accrue after the expiry of the period of fifteen days from the date of receipt of notice by the drawer putting him to knowledge of dishonour by the banker of the cheque which he issued. It is evident that complainant received information about the fact of dishonour of cheque not before 16.02.05 and therefore, legal notice was to be dispatched on or before 18.03.05 (within 30 days). It has been issued on 15.03.05. Now taking the receipt of notice by accused on 16.03.05, when endorsement of "unclaimed" was made, fifteen days expired on 31.03.2005 and Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 10 thus, cause of action for filing the present complaint arose from the next following day, i.e., 01.04.2005 which has to be excluded being the 1st day and count of period of one month ends on 01.05.2005 which has to be included. This is how the period of limitation is counted as explained by the Apex Court in case titled as M/s. Saketh India Ltd. and others v India Securities Ltd. 1999 CRI. L.J. 1822. To sum up, the complaint was filed (29.04.05) two days before the expiry of limitation period and it leads that the contention of the accused that the complaint has been filed after expiry of limitation period is devoid of any merit. 15. Taking into account that the complainant has proved the fact of execution of cheque in question by accused and that the cheque was dishonoured because of funds insufficient in respect of accused's account, he is entitled to and did in fact rely upon the three presumptions in respect of his case, namely, u/s 118, 138 and 139 of the Act and thus it was incumbent upon the accused to rebut these to show his innocence. 16. Now we come to the legal aspect of the case. Law on the point is well settled that the rebuttal cannot be by way of mere denial of liability for issuance of cheque and it has to be by way of proof adduced in the form of evidence to the satisfaction of the Court. Therefore, the burden to prove that the negotiable Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 11 instrument was not issued for consideration lies upon the accused in a prosecution under Section 138 of the Act. In the case of Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai Vs. State of Maharashra {AIR 1964 SC 575}, the Constitution Bench of Supreme Court, while clarifying the distinction between discretionary and mandatory presumption, held that : "In the case of a discretionary presumption the presumption if drawn may be rebutted by an explanation which "might reasonably be true and which is consistent with the innocence" of the accused. On the other hand in the case of a mandatory presumption "the burden resting on the accused person in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under Section 114 of the Evidence Act and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable". It must further be shown that the explanation is a true one. The words 'unless the contrary is proved' which occur in this provision ( Sections 118 and 139 of the Act) make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, the explanation is supported by proof, the mandatory presumption created by the provisions cannot be said to be rebutted." 17. For aforesaid reasons and in light of Apex Court authority mentioned in preceding paragraph, it emerges that accused failed to rebut the presumptions existing in favour of Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 12 complainant. The defence appears to be improbable, insufficient and unconvincing. In the result, accused is convicted of the offence u/s. 138 of the Act. Announced in the open (Vivek Kumar Gulia) court on 14.09.2009 Metropolitan Magistrate-I(E) (total twelve pages) Karkardooma Courts, Delhi. Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 13 IN THE COURT OF SH. VIVEK KUMAR GULIA, METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE - 1 [ East], KARKARDOOMA COURTS, DELHI. In the matter of: Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh C.C. No. 3923/07 PS: Bhajanpura Order on sentence 06.10.2009 Present :-Complainant in person with counsel. Convict Biral Singh on bail with counsel. Arguments heard on the point of sentence. Complainant contended that since convict issued the cheque in discharge of the liability and his guilt has been established beyond any doubt, he be punished with maximum sentence provided. On the other hand, convict submits that as he is first offender and is the only bread earner of his family consisting of his wife and three children of marriageable age. Therefore, it is prayed that a lenient view may be taken. Keeping in view the submissions made on behalf of convict and considering that offence u/s. 138 NI Act has been introduced to encourage greater vigilance to prevent usual callous attitude of drawer of cheque and to lend greater credibility to the greater transactions and lastly that the cases of dishonour of Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 14 cheques are on the high rise in the society, convict is sentenced to simple imprisonment for three months alongwith fine of Rs. 1,52,000/- as per section 143(1) (proviso) N.I. Act r/w section 357(1)(b) of Cr.P.C. Out of this amount, Rs. 1,50,000/- (cheque amount being Rs.1 lac) shall be payable to complainant as compensation and Rs. 2000/- to State within a month from today. In default of payment of fine payable to State, convict shall further undergo simple imprisonment for one month. Further, it is ordered that compensation amount, if not paid in time, it shall be recovered as fine as per provisions of 421 Cr.P.C. At this stage, an application u/s. 389(3) Cr.P.C. for suspension of sentence and grant of bail is moved by convict. Heard. Since the convict intends to present an appeal, he is hereby admitted to bail on furnishing personal bond in the sum of Rs.10,000/- with one surety in the like amount. Bail bond is furnished and accepted. Announced in the open ( Vivek Kumar Gulia ) court on 06.10.2009 MM-I(East)/KKD/Delhi Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07 15 C.C. No. 3923/07 PS: Bhajanpura 06.10.2009 Present:- Parties with their counsel. An application for cancellation of NBW and restoration of bail bond is moved. It is argued that the convict has right to bail since the offence involved is bailable one. In support of this plea, Ld. defence counsel has relied upon the judgment passed by High Court of Delhi reported as 2003 (3) CC Cases (HC) 8. In my considered view, this judgment does not apply on the facts of the case in hand since accused has already been granted bail in this matter which is at the stage of order on sentence. As per section 436 (2) Cr.P.C., accused cannot claim right to bail in a bailable offence once he fails to appear after his release on bail. Still in the interest of justice and considering the nature of offence, application is allowed subject to cost of Rs. 1000/- to be paid to complainant and Rs. 2000/- to be deposited with State. Cost and fine amount paid. Separate order on sentence passed today. Accused has been bailed out u/s. 389(3) Cr.P.C. In case no order from the appellate court is received by ahlmad till 05.11.2009, case file be put up before me for further proceedings. File be consigned to Record Room. (Vivek Kumar Gulia) MM-I (East) KKD Courts Delhi. Tikam Singh Vs. Birbal Singh; CC no. 3923/07
